working_title: Did a Baker Really Burn Down All of London?
hook: We think we know how the Great Fire of London started, but history holds a surprising twist.

scenes.narration: We think we know how the Great Fire of London started, but history holds a surprising twist.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a cozy medieval bakery oven glowing softly in Pudding Lane, warm ochre and deep brick red tones, paper grain visible, calm vertical composition, soft rim light.

scenes.narration: In 1666, the popular story blames Thomas Farriner's bakery for accidentally sparking an unstoppable inferno.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of wooden tenement houses with projecting upper storeys nearly touching across a narrow alley, warm muted palette, gentle depth haze, soft lighting.

scenes.narration: It is true the flames began there just after midnight on Sunday, September second, fed by narrow streets and wooden walls.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of glowing orange flames creeping along timber buildings at night, dark teal shadows, visible paper grain, soft and quiet mood.

scenes.narration: But many believe the Lord Mayor acted instantly to save the city. The evidence tells a different story.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of a worried official in period velvet robes hesitating by a wooden doorway, soft ochre palette, calm vertical framing.

scenes.narration: In reality, Lord Mayor Sir Thomas Bloodworth hesitated for hours, refusing to order crucial house demolitions.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of simple leather buckets and firehooks stacked neatly by a parish church door, quiet street scene, muted teal and brick red tones.

scenes.narration: Some thought it was purely an accident. Yet frightened citizens panicked, and rumors quickly blamed foreign saboteurs.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of silhouetted figures carrying bundles near tall Roman stone walls under a hazy evening sky, visible paper grain.

scenes.narration: People also assume the fire burned unchecked until it simply ran out of fuel.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of the grand dome of Old St Paul's Cathedral glowing against a smoky sky, soft silhouette, warm golden rim light.

scenes.narration: Actually, historians debate the final turning point, but records point to coordinated gunpowder explosions creating vital firebreaks.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of a tall stone column and a distant gilded urn under a calm sky, textured paper grain, warm ochre and teal palette.

scenes.narration: The city rose again from the ashes, keeping its ancient medieval street plan alive today.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of neat brick and timber houses newly built along a winding cobbled lane, warm morning light, peaceful composition.

scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache illustration of a single candle glowing warmly on a wooden table next to an open leather-bound book, calm and inviting mood.

why_it_matters: It separates popular myths about the Great Fire of London from documented historical evidence.
structure: Myth versus fact: state the popular version, then carefully show what the evidence actually says.

claims.claim: We think we know how the Great Fire of London started, but history holds a surprising twist.
claims.note: History generally attributes the start to Thomas Farriner's bakery, but popular narratives often omit the delayed political response or other nuances.

claims.claim: In 1666, the popular story blames Thomas Farriner's bakery for accidentally sparking an unstoppable inferno.
claims.note: The fire started in Thomas Farriner's bakery in Pudding Lane in 1666.

claims.claim: It is true the flames began there just after midnight on Sunday, September second, fed by narrow streets and wooden walls.
claims.note: Started shortly after midnight on Sunday 2 September 1666, fueled by narrow streets, timber construction, and combustibles.

claims.claim: But many believe the Lord Mayor acted instantly to save the city. The evidence tells a different story.
claims.note: The common assumption might be prompt action, but the text explicitly notes the Lord Mayor hesitated.

claims.claim: In reality, Lord Mayor Sir Thomas Bloodworth hesitated for hours, refusing to order crucial house demolitions.
claims.note: Sir Thomas Bloodworth hesitated in giving the order to employ firebreaks through structural removals.

claims.claim: Some thought it was purely an accident. Yet frightened citizens panicked, and rumors quickly blamed foreign saboteurs.
claims.note: Order broke down as rumours arose of suspicious foreigners (French and Dutch) setting fires.

claims.claim: People also assume the fire burned unchecked until it simply ran out of fuel.
claims.note: Refers to a common misconception that the fire only stopped due to lack of fuel, whereas specific interventions ended it.

claims.claim: Actually, historians debate the final turning point, but records point to coordinated gunpowder explosions creating vital firebreaks.
claims.note: Modern historians consider the combination of the wind dying down and the Tower of London garrison using gunpowder to create firebreaks as the winning factors.

claims.claim: The city rose again from the ashes, keeping its ancient medieval street plan alive today.
claims.note: London was reconstructed on essentially the same medieval street plan, which still exists today.

fact_check.summary: Every historical claim made in the narration about the Great Fire of London is fully supported by the reference material.
